Aircraft descended (as commanded) while returning to PLZ resulting in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT).

contributing: power system at maximum output most of the flight in high winds

functions indicating that the Auxiliary FC systems are still operating. This behavior indicates loss of
return to normal function, reducing the likelihood that physical damage caused the initial fault.
They are pushing the maximum allowable windspeed throughout the entire flight and the power draw is high.
the root cause would be that the power system was operating in maximum output conditions for the majority of the flight

team_root_cause:
Root Cause is still under investigation for this incident. Data review yielded a loss of DC current flow between Hybrid Lift System and Fuel Cell Generator as the fault condition that caused the failure, though additional investigation of the equipment is required to provide additional guidance and repair options.
Leading Potential Root Cause Contributing Factors:
·        Failure of individual cells within the HLB.
·        Excessive Current Flow Resulting in Failure of Electrical Hardware.
·        Intermittent Fuel Cell DCDC Regulation Failure.

would_settle_it.what: fuel cell QC test, DCDC regulation check, HLB cell-to-cell voltages and connector/harness inspection; equipment never returned
fuel cell DCDC output current and HLB current at the moment of the 500 W to -26 W drop

reasoning: The AAR shows fuel cell output dropping instantly from 500 W to -26 W while its auxiliary systems kept running, which means current stopped flowing between the fuel cell and the HLB. The report lists HLB cell failure, overcurrent damage to connectors or boards, and fuel cell DCDC regulation failure as candidates and cannot separate them from data. High power demand and a low HLB charge state made the emergency landing fail.
notes: Report summary says the fault was about 98 min 15 s after takeoff, while the timeline says 76 min from launch. Closed because the customer did not return equipment. Another engineer argued the root cause was the operating profile (maximum output, HLB at 40 to 60 percent).

event: On VXE 724 during preflight at flight test, swapping the HLB power-cycled the MCM, resetting the VSM and clearing the uploaded mission; flight was cancelled.
component: SLA Breakout Board 128-117156-01 Rev B, MCM e-fuse (U1 TPS16630) over voltage protection
failure_mode: transient when plugging in the HLB data cable trips the e-fuse over voltage protection set at 34.9 V, dropping MCM supply below its 9 V minimum and rebooting it
contributing: HLB BMS connection bypasses the ground isolation circuit
little transient filtering on the Rev B board

evidence.quote: By using the vehicle web pages, FLOPS was able to determine that the AP had been up ~20 minutes longer than the MCM, indicating a power cycle on MCM.
Initial thought is that there was a transient that exceeded the electronic fuse Over Voltage Protection that is set to 34.9V on the SLA Breakout Board V2.
I was able to test this again with another PreMAG vehicle. It actually showed the same behavior of resetting.
ELECTRONIC-FUSE MCM 2.29A, 34.9V OVER VOLTAGE PROTECTION
Changing values of some of the components of 128-117156-01 so that the E-Fuse is not tripping Over Voltage Protection upon common voltage transient

team_root_cause: SLA Breakout 128-117156-01 Rev B has the Over Voltage Protection pin of both E-Fuses set to ~35V. When plugging in the HLB data cable, transients can occur that may briefly trip the E-Fuse protecting the MCM, which then has the possibility to drop power below the 9V minimum of the MCM.

would_settle_it.file: VXEP 730 - 128-117156-01 Rev B SLA Breakout Board - Increment to Rev C.pptx
would_settle_it.what: scope captures of the e-fuse input and MCM supply during HLB data plug-in

reasoning: Uptime checks showed only the MCM rebooted when the HLB was swapped, and the behavior repeated on another pre-MAGNSS aircraft, so it is a design issue rather than one bad unit. The schematic shows both e-fuses on the Rev B SLA breakout with over voltage protection at 34.9 V, and the fix raised that limit and added filtering. The scope data that confirms the transient is referenced but not in the export, so confidence is medium.
notes: Ticket title originally said 723; vehicle is 724 (pre-MAGNSS) with several other NCRs listed that were not part of this investigation. Rev B boards were not reworked; Rev C cut into production.
